pages.text: The Portuguese India armadas were fleets funded by the Crown of Portugal. They went from Portugal to India every year. Their main destination was Goa. These fleets made the India Run after Vasco da Gama found the sea route in 1497-99.
pages.caption: The large carrack, thought to be the Santa Catarina do Monte Sinai, and other Portuguese carracks of various sizes. From painting, attributed to either Gregório Lopes or Cornelis Antoniszoon, showing voyage of the marriage party of Portuguese Infanta Beatriz to Savoy, 1521.

pages.text: The annual armada was the main carrier of the spice trade between Europe and Asia in the sixteenth century. The Portuguese held a monopoly on this route for a long time. Later, Dutch and English competition broke this monopoly in the early 1600s.

pages.text: The voyage usually took about six months each way. The timing depended on the monsoon winds of the Indian Ocean. The summer winds blew to India, while winter winds blew back to Africa and Portugal. A round trip took a little over a year.
pages.caption: Principal cities of the Swahili Coast of East Africa, c. 1500.

pages.text: The size of the armada changed over time. Early fleets had about fifteen ships. Later, the number went down to five or six ships each year. The ships were usually large carracks. Their sizes grew larger as the years passed.
pages.caption: Padrão of Vasco da Gama, at Malindi, Kenya.

evidence.articleCaption: Padrão of Vasco da Gama, at Malindi, Kenya.

pages.text: Besides carrying troops and officials, the primary goal of the armada was trade. They imported Asian spices to sell in Europe. Captains and crew members were also allowed to trade on their own account to make a personal profit.

B1-B2.headline: Trade and Travel of the India Armadas

pages.text: The Portuguese Indian Armadas were fleets funded by the Crown of Portugal and sent annually to India, primarily to destinations like Goa and Cochin. These fleets performed the Carreira da India after Vasco da Gama discovered the Cape Route in 1497-99.

pages.text: For a century, the Portuguese maintained a monopoly on this spice trade route between Europe and Asia. The dominance lasted until Dutch and English competition breached it in the early 1600s, leading to a subsequent decline in the importance of the armadas.

pages.text: Voyages took approximately six months in each direction, heavily reliant on the seasonal monsoon winds of the Indian Ocean. Ships aimed to pass the Cape of Good Hope around June or July to catch summer monsoons to India, returning in January with winter monsoons.

pages.text: Fleet sizes varied over time, starting with large groups averaging fifteen ships in the first decade, eventually stabilizing at five to six ships annually in the second half of the sixteenth century. The ships themselves were predominantly carracks that grew larger to meet cargo demands.

pages.text: While armadas carried officials and troops, their primary objective was the spice trade, focusing on pepper, cinnamon, cloves, nutmeg, and mace. In addition to royal trade, crew members were permitted to import limited personal cargo volumes free of freight charges.

C1-C2.headline: Mechanics of the Carreira da India

pages.text: Funded by the Portuguese Crown, the India armadas constituted annual fleets dispatched from Lisbon along the Carreira da India. This maritime network was established following Vasco da Gama pioneering the Cape Route to the Indian subcontinent between 1497-99.
pages.caption: The large carrack, thought to be the Santa Catarina do Monte Sinai, and other Portuguese carracks of various sizes. From painting, attributed to either Gregório Lopes or Cornelis Antoniszoon, showing voyage of the marriage party of Portuguese Infanta Beatriz to Savoy, 1521.

pages.text: Serving as the primary conduit for the European-Asian spice trade throughout the sixteenth century, the Portuguese safeguarded a strict monopoly over the Cape route until early seventeenth-century incursions by Dutch and English competitors eroded their dominance and reduced the armadas' strategic significance.
pages.caption: The route of Vasco da Gama's first voyage (1497–1499), what became the typical Carreira da Índia

evidence.articleCaption: The route of Vasco da Gama's first voyage (1497–1499), what became the typical Carreira da Índia

pages.text: Voyage durations averaged six months per leg, dictated strictly by the reversal of Indian Ocean monsoon patterns. Precise timing was vital; missing critical windows off East Africa risked severe delays that could extend a journey by an entire year.
pages.caption: Principal cities of the Swahili Coast of East Africa, c. 1500.

evidence.articleCaption: Principal cities of the Swahili Coast of East Africa, c. 1500.

pages.text: Armada compositions evolved considerably, shifting from initial averages of fifteen vessels per year down to five or six annually by the latter half of the sixteenth century. Concurrently, naval architecture transitioned toward larger carracks designed to maximize cargo capacity.
pages.caption: Padrão of Vasco da Gama, at Malindi, Kenya.

evidence.articleCaption: Padrão of Vasco da Gama, at Malindi, Kenya.

pages.text: The primary commercial objective centered on the importation of core Asian spices. To supplement crown revenues, participating officers and crew members were officially authorized to transport predetermined quantities of private goods within designated liberty chests exempt from standard freight charges and duties.
